commitResults.messageBody:
Add header comments to every class and public method, following the
se-edu format: a summary sentence first, a blank line, then the tags.
Overridden methods are left bare, as the standard allows.

Fix the violations found against the se-edu intermediate standard:
drop two unused imports, rename dayDisplay and asArrayList so method
names are verbs, rename the period array to periodParts, move the event
hint constant up with the other fields, and give the static-only Parser
a private constructor.

Regroup imports across ten files as static, java, third party, own.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CheckStyle: Add Checkstyle to the Gradle build
commitResults.messageBody:
Add the se-edu Checkstyle config under config/checkstyle and apply the
checkstyle plugin, so gradlew build now fails on style violations.

Fix the 18 violations it reported:

- indent the arrow switch cases in Crack and Storage
- give the command switch in Crack an explicit default branch

Add a chat window built with JavaFX, following the JavaFX tutorial:
Launcher starts Main, Main loads MainWindow.fxml, and every message is a
DialogBox. Point mainClass at the launcher so gradlew run opens it.

The window reuses the command handling instead of repeating it. Ui now
sends every line through a print hook, so GuiUi can collect the same
wording for a bubble rather than printing it, and Crack accepts the
interface it should talk through.

The text UI still runs via crack.Crack, which keeps the JUnit tests on
the same code path the window uses.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Varargs: Take several tasks in TaskList.add
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.add now takes varargs, so a caller with a handful of tasks can
hand them over in one call. Callers passing a single task, such as Crack,
are unchanged.

Collapse the runs of add calls in TaskListTest and StorageTest, which is
where building a list several tasks at a time actually happens.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use assertions to document internal assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods rely on assumptions the caller is expected to have
checked already. Crack's markTask, unmarkTask and deleteTask trust that
Parser.parseIndex has bounds-checked the index it hands them, and
TaskDate's constructor trusts that the text it was given parsed cleanly.

None of those assumptions is written down. A future change that breaks
one of them surfaces far from its cause, as an ArrayList index error or
a NullPointerException, which is slow to trace back.

Let's,
* assert the bounds assumption in Crack and TaskList, before an index
  is used to reach into the list
* assert the postcondition of Parser.parseIndex, that a position it
  accepted lands inside the list
* assert that TaskDate never wraps a null date
* enable assertions with -ea on both the test task and the run task

Assertions suit these checks better than exceptions because every one
of them is an internal invariant rather than user input. Bad user input
is already validated and reported through CrackException. Assertions
also cost nothing once disabled, which is how they ship.

commitResults.messageTitle: Improve code quality in Ui, Parser and Storage
commitResults.messageBody:
Three separate weaknesses have built up as the code grew.

Ui.showList and Ui.showFound each carry their own copy of the same
"print these tasks numbered from one, or say there are none" logic. The
two copies have to be kept in step by hand, and they disagree on the
abstraction they accept, one taking a TaskList and the other a list.

Parser splits user input on the literals " /by ", " /from " and " /to "
written out at the point of use. The reader has to work out that these
are command syntax rather than incidental text, and changing the syntax
means hunting down every literal.

Storage.parse returns null to mean "this line is junk". That makes each
caller responsible for a null check, and the signature gives the reader
no hint that null is even possible.

Let's,
* pull the shared listing logic in Ui into one private showNumbered
  method, with each caller passing its own heading and empty message
* name the command markers in Parser as constants
* return Optional<Task> from Storage.parse, and move the type tag
  dispatch into its own buildTask method

Behavior is unchanged. The existing tests still pass and a manual run
of the text interface produces the same output as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams for filtering and keyword lookup
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.find and TaskList.onDate are the same loop written twice: make
an empty list, walk every task, keep the ones meeting a condition, hand
the list back. The loop machinery takes up more room than the condition
that is the only real difference between the two methods.

Command.fromKeyword walks the enum values looking for a match and falls
through to a throw once it runs out. The "no such command" case is
expressed by where the statement sits rather than by what it says.

Let's,
* rewrite both TaskList filters as a stream filter and collect, leaving
  the predicate as the only thing that differs between them
* rewrite Command.fromKeyword as a stream with findFirst and
  orElseThrow, which states the missing case directly

Both filters still collect into an ArrayList, so callers and the
existing tests are unaffected.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add short aliases for command keywords
commitResults.messageBody:
Every command has to be typed out in full. Someone adding several todos
in a row types "todo" each time, and "unmark" and "deadline" are long
enough to be worth shortening for anyone using the app regularly.

Command already owns the mapping from a typed word to a command, so the
change belongs there and nowhere else. Nothing outside the enum needs
to know whether the user typed an alias or the full name.

Let's,
* give the enum constructor varargs, so each command lists its full
  name first and any aliases after it
* widen the lookup in fromKeyword from an equality check to a
  membership check over that list
* add t, d, e, ls, m, um, rm, del and f as aliases

Full names keep working, so nothing a user already types breaks. Delete
takes rm and del rather than d, because d is worth more to deadline,
the longer of the two words.

CommandTest covers each alias, checks that every word a command claims
resolves back to that command, and guards against two commands claiming
the same word. Without that guard a clash would be resolved silently by
enum declaration order.

Both sides of the conversation were drawn the same way: a rounded bubble
built from inline styles, differing only in color and which edge it hugged.
Errors looked exactly like ordinary replies, so a rejected command was easy
to scroll past.

Move the styling out to view/main.css and give each speaker its own shape:

* Crack speaks from the left behind a circular avatar and a name label, in
  a light card whose corner nearest the avatar is squared off.
* The user speaks from the right as a bare accent bubble, mirrored.
* A reply that reports a problem gets a tinted bubble, a red rule down its
  left edge and a warning avatar.

GuiUi now hands back a Reply record carrying both the text and whether the
turn produced an error, so the window picks the right bubble without
depending on the order in which it reads the two.

Bubbles wrap against a share of the row width rather than a fixed 300px, so
they follow the window as it is resized. The input row is its own bar, and
the scroll pane, text field and send button are styled to match.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Personality: Commit to one voice across app
commitResults.messageBody:
Crack half sounded like a character and half sounded like a form validator.
The confirmations had slang in them, but the format hints and the save
failure were written in plain English, and the window was office blue and
white, which matched neither.

Give the same character to all three surfaces the increment names:

* Phrases: every line Crack says now reads in one voice, including the
  '/by' and '/from' hints in Parser and the unreadable-save-file complaint
  in Storage, which were the last two flat ones. Wording follows how the
  slang is actually used rather than how it looks: vocatives like 'gng' sit
  at the end of the sentence, 'ts' takes the subject slot, and 'icl' opens
  one.
* Colors and font: the window goes dark and high contrast with a violet
  accent, and the avatar picks up a violet-to-pink gradient that turns red
  when the reply is a complaint.
* Name: a header bar puts the product name at the top of the window, so it
  is visible in the app itself and not only in the title bar.

Add a help command, since a chatbot with nine aliases and no way to list
them leaves the personality talking to itself. Command now carries the
argument shape and a one-line summary next to the keywords it already held,
so help is generated from the enum and a new command shows up in it without
anyone remembering to update a second list. The constants are reordered to
read in that listing: adding, then looking up, then changing. Unknown input
now points at help instead of just complaining.

GuiUiTest no longer pins the exact goodbye wording. It was the only test
that would break every time a phrase was reworded, and the flag it actually
covers is whether the reply was an error.

Both sides of the conversation are drawn the same way: a rounded bubble
built from inline styles, differing only in color and which edge it
hugs. A reply reporting a problem is drawn identically to any other.

The conversation is between a person and an app, not between two
people, so drawing both sides alike misrepresents what it is. It also
leaves a rejected command easy to scroll past, which is the one reply
the user most needs to catch.

Merge branch-A-BetterGui, which moves the styling out to view/main.css
and gives each speaker a shape of its own:

* Crack speaks from the left behind a circular avatar and a name label.
* The user speaks from the right as a bare accent bubble, mirrored.
* A reply that reports a problem gets a tinted bubble, a red rule down
  its left edge and a warning avatar.

The look lives in a stylesheet rather than in Java so it can be changed
without touching the view classes, which the personality increment
depends on. GuiUi hands back a record carrying the text together with
whether the turn errored, so the window cannot read the two out of
order and paint the wrong bubble.

47 tests pass, up from 43. Checkstyle is clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle common input and date errors gracefully
commitResults.messageBody:
Four unintentional user errors are either accepted silently or refused
for no good reason.

A date that does not exist is not rejected: the parser resolves leniently,
so 'deadline x /by 30-2-2026' is stored as Feb 28. Quietly filing a task
under a date the user did not type is worse than refusing the input. An
event whose end precedes its start is accepted whole, giving a task that
can never be worked on. A blank line, which is the easiest thing to send
by accident, draws the same complaint as a misspelt command. A command
typed in the wrong case is refused outright, though phone keyboards
capitalise a first word by default.

Refuse what cannot be meant and accept what plainly can:

* Parse dates strictly, so an impossible day is reported rather than
  nudged to a real one. Strict resolution needs the proleptic year
  'uuuu' in place of 'yyyy'.
* Reject an event that ends before it starts. Equal endpoints stay legal,
  since a one day event is written that way.
* Ignore a blank line instead of answering it.
* Match the command word without regard to case, against Locale.ROOT so
  the mapping does not shift with the user's locale.
* Split the command word off on any run of whitespace, so a stray space
  or a tab no longer hides it.

Report a failed save after the confirmation rather than before it, so the
warning reads as belonging to the command that triggered it.

A saved event with reversed dates is now dropped on load, along with the
other unreadable lines. Only this build could have written one.

56 tests pass, up from 51. Checkstyle is clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Fix data loss and a crash on save
commitResults.messageBody:
A saved line is split on every " | " it contains, and the description is
read as the third field. Nothing stops a description holding that
separator, and ordinary text does: 'todo email bob | cc alice' saves
cleanly, displays correctly, and comes back as 'email bob' after a
restart. A deadline or an event written the same way disappears
altogether, because the shifted fields no longer parse as dates. The
loss is silent and only shows up on the next run, which is the worst
way to find it.

Take the date fields off the end of the line instead of counting fields
from the front. A date never contains the separator, so the trailing
fields are unambiguous no matter what the description holds, and the
description is simply whatever is left. Old save files still load, since
the layout has not changed.

Two smaller faults in the same file:

* A line carrying a blank description loads as a task with no text,
  which the input path would never allow. Skip those lines like any
  other unreadable one.
* save() calls mkdirs() on the parent folder without checking there is
  one, so a path naming no folder throws NullPointerException instead of
  saving. Only save through the app avoids this today, and a crash is a
  poor way to report it.

59 tests pass, up from 56. Checkstyle is clean.

Crack accepts several things the user cannot have meant, refuses a few
they plainly did, and loses tasks outright between runs.

Seven faults, found by running the app against bad input rather than by
reading the code:

* A date that does not exist resolves leniently, so a deadline set for
  30 Feb is filed under 28 Feb without a word.
* An event whose end precedes its start is accepted whole.
* A blank line, the easiest thing to send by accident, draws the same
  complaint as a misspelt command.
* A command typed in the wrong case is refused, though phone keyboards
  capitalise a first word by default.
* A description holding " | " breaks the save format, so a todo returns
  truncated and a deadline or event disappears. The loss is silent and
  surfaces only on the next run.
* A saved line with a blank description loads as a task with no text.
* Saving to a path that names no folder throws NullPointerException.

Merge finalize-features, which refuses what cannot be meant, accepts
what plainly can, and stops the save file losing anything. Date fields
are now taken off the end of a saved line rather than counted from the
front: a date never contains the separator and a description may, so
only the end is unambiguous. Old save files load unchanged.

Storage was already sound elsewhere and is left as it stands. A missing
file starts a fresh list, unreadable lines are skipped one by one, and
an unwritable folder is reported without ending the session. The
product name was checked across every surface it appears on and needed
no change.

59 tests pass, up from 51. Checkstyle is clean.

Both READMEs are still the ones the project shipped with. The page the
product website publishes, docs/README.md, is placeholder headings, and
the root README describes a greenfield template. Anyone landing on
either learns neither what Crack is nor how to talk to it.

Write the guide the site will publish. It opens with a table of every
command and a handful of lines to paste in, so a reader can be using
Crack before they have read any of it. Below that each command gets its
format, an example, and the output that example actually produces,
lifted from a real session rather than written from memory, so the page
cannot drift from the product without someone noticing. Dates, the
errors Crack answers with and where the save file lives round it out.

Bring the root README up to date and hold it to building and running:
setting up in IntelliJ, the Gradle tasks, text mode, and which directory
the save file lands in. Usage belongs to the guide, and each page links
to the other. Splitting them this way leaves one page to correct when a
command changes, rather than two that quietly disagree.

Add docs/Ui.png, the screenshot the guide opens with. It is rendered off
the scene graph rather than captured off a display, so it comes out at
twice size with nothing but the window in it.

Stop tracking docs/git-stuff.txt and ignore it from here on. It is a
scratch file of git notes, tracked since Level-8, and the site serves
everything under docs/, so once Pages is switched on it would be
published as a page of its own. The file stays on disk untouched.

Neither README has been touched since the project was generated. The one
the product website publishes is a page of placeholder headings, and the
one on the repo front page describes a greenfield template. There is no
picture of the product anywhere.

Someone arriving at the site cannot find out what Crack is, which
commands it takes or how to write a date. Someone arriving
cannot tell that the two pages are meant for different readers, because
both currently answer neither question.

Merge branch-A-UserGuide, which gives each page one job:

* docs/README.md becomes the user guide the site publishes. It opens
  with a table of every command and seven lines to paste in
  through each command with its format, an example and the output that
  example gives back. Dates, the errors Crack answers with and where
  the save file lives follow.
* README.md keeps the repo front page and is held to building and
  running: IntelliJ setup, the Gradle tasks, text mode.
* docs/Ui.png is the screenshot the guide opens with, rendered off the
  scene graph rather than captured off a display.

Every example output is lifted from a real session rather t
from memory, so the page cannot drift from the product without someone
noticing.

docs/git-stuff.txt stops being tracked in the same breath. Pages serves
everything under docs/, so a scratch file left there goes o
